FLOWS.t: Why Indian civil services resist change
s: Aristocratic personnel system: sharp grade divide, narrow age band, general-ability exams, cadre-based
Closed career: conservative, status quoist, rule fetishism, rank over competence
Elitist mindset: obstacles to change
Plus: traditional education, limited mobility, political failure, poverty
Result: slow pace of social change
Fix: lateral entry, specialisation after 10-12 years
Single Directive: sanction needed even for preliminary inquiry against Joint Secretary and above
1997 Vineet Narain: Supreme Court strikes the Single Directive
DSPE Act amended: Single Directive made law as Sec 6A
2014: Sec 6A struck down (equality)
2018: PCA Sec 17A: permission for preliminary inquiry for all public servants, except if caught red-handed (extends to retired servants)
Meanwhile: PCA Sec 19 and CrPC Sec 197 still need sanction to prosecute; Lokpal replaces the sanctioning authority in its cases
Any individual files a complaint for a PCA 1988 offence
Lokpal orders a preliminary inquiry (Inquiry Wing, CVC or CBI) and seeks the public servant's explanation
Complaints against Group C and D officials go to the CVC
Preliminary inquiry finishes within 60 days
Lokpal bench (min 3) hears the public servant, then: full investigation, departmental proceedings, close the case, or act against a false complainant
If PM is the accused: full bench, two-thirds majority; not public order, security, atomic energy, space
Prosecution wing and court; time limit for the complaint: 7 years

TRAPS.t: FPSC: Act year is not set-up year
TRAPS.d: The 1919 Act provided for a Federal PSC; it was set up in 1926 on the Lee Commission (1924). Madras (1929) was the first provincial PSC.
TRAPS.r: Rule: when asked 'set up', use the establishment date, not the Act date.

TRAPS.d: Nine AIS in 1909, four in 1924, two in 1947, three today (IAS, IPS, IFoS).
TRAPS.r: Rule: pin the number to its year before choosing.

TRAPS.d: Art 312 creates AIS; 315-323 cover PSCs; 309-311 service conditions, tenure, dismissal; 323A administrative tribunals; Art 16 equality in public employment.
TRAPS.r: Rule: Arts 309-311 = the servant, 315-323 = the Commission, 312 = the All India Service.

TRAPS.t: Steel Frame and Father of AIS
TRAPS.d: Lloyd George used 'Steel Frame' for the Imperial Civil Service. Patel is the Father of All India Services.
TRAPS.r: Rule: the phrase and the person are different people.

TRAPS.d: CIC: 3 years or 65 (2019 Rules). CVC: 4 years or 65. Lokpal: 5 years or 70.
TRAPS.r: Rule: Lokpal is the longest; CIC changed in 2019.

TRAPS.d: Lokpal has the Speaker and an eminent jurist; CVC has the Home Minister; CBI Director's committee has the CJI; CIC has a Union Cabinet Minister (2nd ARC wants the CJI).
TRAPS.r: Rule: PM and Leader of Opposition are in all; learn the third and fourth members.

TRAPS.d: Lokpal removal reference to the SC needs signatures of at least 100 MPs. CIC/CVC go to the SC on the President's reference.
TRAPS.r: Rule: '100 MPs' belongs only to Lokpal.

TRAPS.d: 5 days: transfer; 10 days: third-party notice; 30 days: reply; 100 days: designate PIOs; 120 days: publish 16 types; 20 years: release exempted records; Rs 250 a day up to Rs 25,000.
TRAPS.r: Rule: write the unit with each number.

TRAPS.d: Copyright held by a person other than the State is the only absolute exemption. Sec 8(2) lets public interest override the rest; the Second Schedule agencies still owe information on corruption and human rights.
TRAPS.r: Rule: 'absolute' appears only with copyright.

TRAPS.d: Sweden 1766 (RTI) and 1809 (ombudsman); USA second (1966); Tamil Nadu first state RTI law (1997); Maharashtra first Lokayukta (1971).
TRAPS.r: Rule: Sweden twice, USA second.

TRAPS.d: A Charter creates no new rights; it enforces existing ones. Launched in the UK in 1991. Sevottam: 2nd ARC concept, launched 2006, IS 15700:2005, pilots 2009-10.
TRAPS.r: Rule: Charter = promise; right = already existing.

TRAPS.d: No anonymous complaints under the 2014 Act; frivolous complaint: 2-year jail; competent authority depends on who is accused.
TRAPS.r: Rule: no anonymity is the first answer to 'what is wrong with the Act'.

TRAPS.d: Bribe-giving an offence (7-day complaint defence for coercion), jail 3 to 7 years, trial 2 years (max 4), Sec 17A covers retired servants; yet Sec 13(1)(d) was diluted and Sec 17A needs permission for inquiry.
TRAPS.r: Rule: strengthened punishment, weakened investigation.

TRAPS.d: CPI: 0 most corrupt, 100 least; perception-based; since 1995; ranks not comparable across years. Global Corruption Barometer is experiential and regional; PETS is a World Bank tracking survey.
TRAPS.r: Rule: perception (CPI), experience (GCB), tracking (PETS).

TRAPS.t: UPSC is constitutional but not equal
TRAPS.d: UPSC is listed among four important constitutional bodies yet has no separate oath and an easier removal process. Convention on the Chairman broken in 2015.
TRAPS.r: Rule: independence is protected by pay and removal rules, not by status.

TRAPS.d: Political neutrality does not mean policy neutrality. Officers advise intellectually, not emotionally.
TRAPS.r: Rule: understand politics, do not play politics.

TRAPS.d: Module 1 says India appointed an ombudsman in 2013 at the central level. Module 2 says the Act was passed in 2013 and the Lokpal constituted in 2019.
TRAPS.r: Rule: Act 2013; Lokpal constituted 2019.

TRAPS.t: Lokpal's reach over Groups C and D
TRAPS.d: Module 2 lists Group A-D in Lokpal's jurisdiction but sends Group C and D complaints to the CVC.
TRAPS.r: Rule: Lokpal covers them on paper; the CVC handles those complaints.

TRAPS.d: Module 1 names CAG, CBI and CVC in one table and CAG, EC, CVC, CIC, ombudsman in another.
TRAPS.r: Rule: name CAG and CVC always; add the rest as asked.

TRAPS.d: The 2014, 2017 and 2020 questions in Module 1 are printed without marks; 2017 and 2020 give word limits (250 and 150).
TRAPS.r: Rule: plan the 2014-type answer at 10-15 marks from the notes, check the paper's marks on the day.

TRAPS.t: Several PYQs sit outside these modules
TRAPS.d: Public Examination Act 2024 (M2 p.20), Satyam 2009 (p.21) and DBT 2022 (one line only) are not covered; the CBI 2021 question needs state-consent material not in the notes.

PYQS.q: Has the cadre-based Civil Services organization been the cause of slow change in India? Critically examine.
PYQS.trap: Cadre system is one cause among several. Do not make it the only one.

sk.i: Cadre-based, closed career services are part of what the handout calls an aristocratic personnel system.
b: Features: sharp grade divide, narrow age band, general-ability exams, class preference, cadre-based services
Consequences: conservative, status quoist, non-responsive, rule fetishism, rank over competence, elitist, obstacles to change
Other causes listed: traditional education, conservative attitudes to women, limited mobility, failure of the political system, poverty
Fixes: lateral entry, specialisation after 10-12 years, domainisation
sk.c: The cadre system is a major brake on change, but not the only one; reform of services must go with political and social reform.

PYQS.q: Initially Civil Services in India were designed to achieve the goals of neutrality and effectiveness, which seems to be lacking in the present context. Do you agree with the view that drastic reforms are required in Civil Services? Comment.
PYQS.trap: Cover both neutrality and effectiveness, then reforms. Do not list only reforms.

sk.i: Neutrality (class, cultural, political) and effectiveness are both strained.
b: Neutrality: middle-class mindset, political pressure, Ghose's 'weather report readers', politicised transfers
Effectiveness: average DC tenure about one year, poor training (one in five trained), no quantifiable appraisal, 'hire, but no fire'
Reform: tenure security and Civil Services Boards (T.S.R. Subramanian 2013); comprehensive Civil Services Law; 360-degree appraisal; domainisation; lateral entry
Mission Karmayogi: roles-based competency, iGOT, outcome-based appraisal
sk.c: Reform needs to be continuous and structural, not drastic: protect neutrality, reward results.

PYQS.q: "Institutional quality is a crucial driver of economic performance". In this context suggest reforms in Civil Service for strengthening democracy.
PYQS.trap: 150 words: three or four crisp reforms, each tied to democracy.

sk.i: Quality civil services (a key institution) support performance and democracy.
b: Recruitment: lateral entry, psycho-social profile, probation
Training and competency: mid-career training, Mission Karmayogi (rules to roles)
Appraisal and tenure: outcome-based, 360-degree, stable tenure
Openness: RTI, Citizens' Charters, social audit; Nolan Principles
sk.c: A competent, neutral and accountable service is the institution that carries democracy to citizens.

PYQS.q: The Citizens' charter has been a land mark initiative in ensuring citizen-centric administration. But it is yet to reach its full potential. Identify the factors hindering the realisation of its promise and suggest measures to overcome them.
PYQS.trap: Two halves: factors AND measures. Give both equal space.

sk.i: A Charter commits an organisation to quality and time standards for existing rights (UK, 1991); it creates no new rights.
b: Factors: limited consultation (manager's charter), no penal provisions, low awareness, standards too lax or strict, no names of redressal functionaries, no incentives, weak review, no devolution to street-level staff, jargon and no vernacular
Measures: separate charter per unit and service, widest consultation, commit only to what can be delivered, redressal mechanism, periodic evaluation with end-user feedback, penal provisions
Institutional: outside-agency review, Charter Mark-type incentives, Sevottam (IS 15700:2005), digital link with CPGRAMS
sk.c: A charter works when promises are realistic, owned by frontline staff and measured by someone outside.

PYQS.q: Citizens' Charter is an ideal instrument of organizational transparency and accountability, but it has its own limitations. Identify the limitations and suggest measures for greater effectiveness of the Citizens Charter.
PYQS.trap: Open by saying why it is an ideal instrument (transparency, accountability) before limitations.

sk.i: A Charter makes standards and timelines public, so performers can be told from non-performers.
b: Limitations: no penal provisions, limited consultation, unrealistic standards, awareness gap, no incentives, brochures taken as charters, poor review
Measures: hand-holding by DARPG for first charters, mandatory user and staff involvement, outside monitoring, simplified language, 5-year master plan with budget
Sevottam adds three modules (charter, grievance redress, service capability)
sk.c: Transparency of promise must be matched by consequence for failure.

PYQS.q: Though Citizen's charters have been formulated by many public service delivery organizations, there is no corresponding improvement in the level of citizens' satisfaction and quality of services being provided. Analyze.
PYQS.trap: 'Analyze' means give reasons for the gap between charters and satisfaction.

sk.i: By end 2011 there were 131 central and 729 state charters, but numbers are not outcomes.
b: Charters without penalties or incentives do not change behaviour
Standards set without checking resources and workload lose public confidence
Charters not known to citizens; jargon; same format for all services
Weak review and updating; grievance functionaries not named
Fix: ARC-II 'commit to what you can deliver', reform internal processes, hold officers accountable
sk.c: Satisfaction follows delivery capacity, not the number of charters issued.

PYQS.q: What are the aims and objects of the recently passed and enforced, The Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024? Whether University/State Education Board examinations, too, are covered under the Act?
PYQS.trap: No content in these two modules. Do not answer from the notes.

PYQS.q: Reforming the government delivery system through the Direct Benefit Transfer Scheme is a progressive step, but it has its limitations too. Comment.
PYQS.trap: The modules mention DBT only once (privacy). Build the answer elsewhere.
PYQS.partial: Only line in the modules: data privacy concerns in e-governance such as Aadhaar and DBT need strong data protection frameworks; digital and language barriers can exclude marginalised groups (M1 p.23).

PYQS.q: "Recent amendments to the Right to Information Act will have profound impact on the autonomy and independence of the Information Commission". Discuss.
PYQS.trap: Give both negative and positive implications, then a verdict.

sk.i: The RTI Amendment Act 2019 moved tenure, salary and service conditions of the CIC and ICs from the Act to executive rules.
b: What changed: Centre decides tenure (five-year term removed); fixes salary and conditions, delinked from CEC and ECs; CIC clarified as statutory
Negative: executive overreach, public distrust, federal dilution of SICs
Positive: administrative flexibility, fiscal discipline, policy alignment
Now: tenure 3 years or age 65; CIC Rs 2.5 lakh, IC Rs 2.25 lakh; removal still needs SC inquiry
sk.c: The impact turns on how responsibly the government uses its new powers.

PYQS.q: Effectiveness of the government system at various levels and people's participation in the governance system are inter-dependent. Discuss their relationship with each other in context of India.
PYQS.partial: Partial fit: notes cover participation tools, not a theory of the relationship.
PYQS.trap: Show both directions: participation improves effectiveness, effectiveness invites participation.

sk.i: Participation tools turn citizens into monitors of government performance.
b: Social audit, Citizen Report Cards, public hearings, public expenditure tracking improve service quality and deter corruption
Charters and RTI give citizens the information to participate; MKSS jan sunwais led to RTI
AP SSAAT and Bengaluru report cards show effectiveness gains; participation in Charter design is a 'key element of democracy'
Limits: low awareness (RTI), no trained auditors, digital divide
sk.c: Effective government invites participation, and participation keeps government effective.

PYQS.q: In the integrity index of Transparency International, India stands very low. Discuss briefly the legal, political, economic, social and cultural factors that have caused the decline of public morality in India.
PYQS.trap: Five headings asked. Give each one at least one point.

sk.i: TI's index is perception-based, but the handout's factor list explains a low rating.
b: Legal: Art 311 protection, Sec 19 PCA and Sec 197 CrPC sanctions, delayed prosecution, no effective whistleblower law, weak autonomy of CBI and CVC
Political: no will on Lokpal, criminalisation of politics, money power, weak party-funding disclosure, TINA
Economic: licence-permit-quota to clearance raj, consumerism, poor pay, MNC willingness to bribe
Social: shaming of government staff, no popular sanction, social evils like dowry, thymos (low self-worth)
Cultural: long history of corruption, tolerance, culture-specific norms
sk.c: Public morality will recover only when opportunity, impunity and tolerance fall together.

PYQS.q: If amendment bill to the Whistleblowers Act, 2011 tabled in the Parliament is passed, there may be no one left to protect. Critically evaluate.
PYQS.trap: The modules give only one line on the 2015 bill (OSA override). Say so; build the rest from the Act's gaps.

sk.i: The 2015 amendment bill proposed that the Official Secrets Act 1923 would override the Act; it lapsed.
b: Protection already weak: no anonymity (Satyendra Dubey murder), limited safeguards against victimisation
Competent authority route: PM, CM, Presiding Officer, CVC
Frivolous complaints face 2-year jail
Fixes: Law Commission framework (confidentiality, anonymity, protection from bodily harm, corporate whistleblowers); SEBI tipping up to Rs 1 crore
sk.c: A whistleblower law that yields to the Official Secrets Act protects secrecy, not the whistleblower.

PYQS.q: In the light of the Satyam Scandal (2009), discuss the changes brought in corporate governance to ensure transparency, accountability.
PYQS.trap: No content in these two modules. Do not answer from the notes.

PYQS.q: 'A national Lokpal, however strong it may be, cannot resolve the problems of immorality in public affairs'. Discuss.
PYQS.trap: Agree, but show what Lokpal does contribute.

sk.i: The handout calls Lokpal 'not a panacea': corruption is a hydra-headed monster.
b: Needs a multi-pronged strategy; huge bureaucracy; petty complaints need departmental handling
Judicial process inadequate; no citizen empowerment or willingness to complain
Causes of immorality are psycho-social, economic, legal, administrative and political (Sec 15)
What Lokpal adds: inquiry and prosecution wings, search, seizure, attachment, sanction replaced
sk.c: Institutions police conduct; immorality is cured by opportunity reduction, transparency and ethics.

PYQS.q: The jurisdiction of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) regarding lodging an FIR and conducting a probe within a particular State is being questioned by various States. However, the power of the States to withhold consent to the CBI is not absolute. Explain with special reference to the federal character of India.
PYQS.partial: Partial fit: no content on state consent or federal case law.
PYQS.trap: Notes give only CBI's structure (DSPE Act, no suo motu jurisdiction). Add the federal argument from other sources.

sk.i: CBI draws its powers from the DSPE Act 1946 and has no suo motu jurisdiction; it handles cases transferred to it.
b: Vineet Narain 1997: CVC superintends CBI on PCA cases; DoPT sets only policy
Issues: politicised 'caged parrot', one-third vacancies
Federal angle: not in the modules, so add it separately
sk.c: State consent protects federalism but cannot be used to block corruption probes.

PYQS.q: An independent and empowered social audit mechanism is an absolute must in every sphere of public service, including the judiciary, to ensure performance, accountability and ethical conduct. Elaborate.
PYQS.trap: Address the judiciary explicitly (M1 p.33: SC held judiciary by and large covered by RTI, 2019).

sk.i: Social audit shares scheme details with beneficiaries at public hearings so the people can find loopholes.
b: Independence: AP's SSAAT, Karnataka's rotation of audit teams after three cycles, Meghalaya 2017 Act as model
Empowerment: statutory in very few programmes (NREGA); needs trained auditors, Gram Sabha awareness, digital portals
Results: crores recovered in AP; Jharkhand SAU exposed ghost beneficiaries; SC in Swaraj Abhiyan (2016)
Judiciary: RTI coverage held in 2019, but the notes give no audit model for it
sk.c: Audit works when information is open and the auditor is independent of the audited.

PYQS.q: Whistle blower, who reports corruption and illegal activities, wrongdoing and misconduct to the concerned authorities, runs the risk of being exposed to grave danger, physical harm and victimization by the vested interests, accused persons and his team. What policy measures would you suggest to strengthen protection mechanism to safeguard the whistle blower?
PYQS.trap: Policy measures asked: list measures, not the history of the Act.

sk.i: The 2014 Act mandates disclosure of identity and offers limited protection; Satyendra Dubey's murder shows the risk.
b: Confidentiality and anonymity (Law Commission framework)
Legal protection against victimisation and administrative safeguards against harassment and bodily harm
Extend coverage to corporate whistleblowers; 2nd ARC: stronger law for public and private sectors
Organisational guidelines and awareness; SEBI-style rewards up to Rs 1 crore; CVC power to direct protection
sk.c: Protect the person, not just the disclosure.

PYQS.q: "Non-performance of duty by a public servant is a form of corruption" Do you agree with this view? Justify your answer.
PYQS.trap: 150 words: take a position in the first line.

sk.i: Agree, in the wider sense: corruption includes any behaviour that harms public interest.
b: Handout list: lethargy, dereliction or negligence of duty, repeated carelessness, non-punctuality, favouritism and nepotism
TI's definition ('private abuse of public office') and the Elephant Test: society recognises it
Non-performance harms citizens like speed money does (white corruption tolerated)
Caveat: stretching the definition too wide dilutes focus
sk.c: A public servant who does not perform abuses the office for a private ease.

PYQS.q: It is often said that poverty leads to corruption. However, there is no dearth of instances where affluent and powerful people indulge in corruption in a big way. What are the basic causes of corruption among people? Support your answer with examples.
PYQS.trap: Contrast need-based and greed/opportunity-based corruption, with examples.

sk.i: Poor pay is blamed, but the handout says raising salaries alone may not dent corruption.
b: Psycho-social: thymos (low self-worth), consumerism, Squirrel Nuts Syndrome, opportunity theory
Policy (grand) corruption: crony capitalism and state capture by business houses; MNCs able and willing to bribe
Systemic: clearance raj, red tape, middlemen, weak sanctions (Art 311, Sec 19)
Examples in the handout: Mundhra scandal, pork-barreling, German car insurance case
sk.c: Opportunity and impunity, not poverty, are the common thread.

SECS.title: Civil Services: UPSC and SPSC
SECS.story: Part XIV (Arts 308-323) gives the country its Public Service Commissions. They began with the 1919 Act and the 1926 FPSC, and are protected by constitutional safeguards, yet governments deviate from their advice and the UPSC lacks the status of the other constitutional bodies.

prelims: FPSC set up in 1926 (Lee Commission, 1924); Madras 1929 first provincial PSC; Sir Ross Barker first chairman
Article numbers 315-323 and what each covers
Seniority convention for UPSC Chairman broken in 2015
mains: Why the UPSC does not enjoy equal status with EC, CAG and SC (no separate oath, easier removal)
Negative recruitment; two 2nd ARC models for compressing the exam cycle

Need for transparency and accountability
lens.close: Move from top-down, input-focused control to bottom-up, outcome-focused answerability.

notes: Responsibility = obligation to carry out assigned tasks. Accountability = responsibility operating hierarchically; answerability for one's actions. Two aspects: answerability (account) and enforceability (penalty).

Components: answerability, enforcement, responsiveness. Values: integrity, impartiality, objectivity, empathy and compassion. Dimensions: controlling political power, informational, argumentative, human.
Objectives: control abuse; performance standards; continuous improvement; link administration and democracy; institutional introspection.

head: Type
Meaning
rows: Within the hierarchy: superiors and subordinates
Civil servants to political executive, who answer to the legislature
Enforced by external institutions: CAG, CBI, CVC
Codes enforced by bodies like the Bar Council or ICAI
Citizens via RTI, Citizens' Charters, social audits and Lokpal

notes: Accountable to: hierarchy, legislature, judiciary, citizens and civil society, media. Intra-organisational (within) vs inter/extra-organisational (outside).

head: Form
Detail
rows: State institutions that seek explanations and impose penalties: CAG, Election Commission, CVC, CIC, ombudsman
Citizens and civil society: elections, lobbying, budgeting participation, Citizen Report Cards, social audits
One of the oldest; scrutiny of accounts; legislature's power over the public purse. World Bank: accounting system, external audit, follow-up on findings
How agencies perform tasks; tenders, contracts
Results and effectiveness, e.g. beneficiaries identified correctly and living standards improved
Doctors, engineers: professional codes and public interest
Beyond obedience to rules; moral government

notes: World Bank: micro-accountability (responsiveness to citizens receiving services) and macro-accountability (financial and economic performance).
Need: expanding government role; delegated legislation; politics-bureaucracy nexus; corruption; limited popular participation.

How to ensure: traditional (ministerial control, debates, committees, media, ombudsman) and New Public Management (efficiency, outcomes, competition, value for money). Three questions: accountability for what, to whom, through what.

CVC: set up Feb 1964 on the Santhanam Committee; statutory under the CVC Act 2003. Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013: Selection Committee: PM, Lok Sabha Speaker, Leader of Opposition (LS), CJI or nominated SC judge, eminent jurist.

Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014: mechanism for complaints on corruption or wilful misuse of power; inquiry; safeguards against victimisation; anonymous complaints not entertained. CAG: 'guardian of the public purse'; reports go to Parliament and the PAC. Social audit, RTI, Citizens' Charters.
Modern mechanisms: performance audits and outcome budgeting; Social Audit 2.0 (digital dashboards); ethics committees; data-driven vigilance cells; CPGRAMS and PRAGATI.
Issues: unclear relationships; size of government; expanded state activity; secrecy; excess focus on inputs; top-down enforcement; control of bureaucratic power.
New-age challenges: algorithmic governance and AI bias; platform governance; decentralised social media; PPPs diffusing accountability (blame-shifting).

Solutions: decentralisation (World Bank); resilient mechanisms; compliance; bottom-up accountability; adapt to digitalisation; value-driven responsibility; ethical capacity building; internalise accountability beyond fear of sanction; technology with human oversight.

SECS.title: Citizen's Charter and Sevottam
SECS.src: Handout only; three PYQs quoted in Module 2 (2013, 2018, 2024)
SECS.story: A Charter promises quality and time for existing rights. India's charters fail because of limited consultation, no penalties, low awareness, over- or under-tight standards and jargon. ARC-II and Sevottam (2006) supply the fix: separate charters, realistic commitments, redressal, feedback, outside review.

prelims: Launched 1991 by John Major government (UK); creates no new rights
Seven elements of an Indian charter
By end 2011: 131 central, 729 state charters; goicharters.nic.in
Sevottam: 2nd ARC, launched 2006; pilots 2009-10; IS 15700:2005 (BIS); three modules; seven steps
UK Charter Mark scheme
mains: Problems with the Indian programme and suggestions
ARC-II recommendations
Sevottam: significance, challenges, way forward
lens.close: Commit only to what you can deliver, say who is accountable, and measure it through someone outside.

notes: Launched in 1991 by the John Major government (UK). A declaration of an organisation's commitment to clients on qualitative and temporal entitlements. It does not create new rights; it seeks enforcement of existing rights and includes grievance redress.

Clarifies expectations; makes government responsive; service orientation over master mindset; people's participation via consultation; strengthens accountability (quality standards and timelines let performers be distinguished); signals pro-active good governance; improves image and credibility; empowerment and democracy; instrument for development goals.

Vision and mission; details of business transacted; details of clients served; services to each client group; grievance redressal machinery and how to access it; expectations from clients (documents, fees); compensation details. Regular internal and external monitoring. By 2011 end: 131 central charters, 729 state charters. Website goicharters.nic.in.

Bureaucratic mindset; limited consultation (a manager's charter); no penal provisions; low awareness; standards too lax or too strict; too detailed or too brief; names and addresses of redressal functionaries missing; no incentives (UK Charter Mark; DARPG hired an outside agency); brochures and manuals treated as charters (DARPG now directs separate lists); needs of senior citizens and the disabled ignored; poor review and updating; inadequate devolution to street-level staff; technical jargon, no vernacular; same format for every service.

DARPG hand-holding for first charters; awareness (credible NGOs); attitudinal change; mandatory involvement of user groups and staff; built-in monitoring, preferably by an outside agency; prioritise services; incentivise at organisation and individual level; showcase best practices; simple language; 5-year master plan with budget.

One size does not fit all (separate charter per unit and service); widest consultation; commit to what you can deliver; reform internal processes; appropriate redressal; periodic evaluation with end-user feedback; hold officers accountable for results (penal provisions).
Conceptualised by the 2nd ARC, launched 2006; piloted in ten departments (2009-10); IS 15700:2005 by the Bureau of Indian Standards certifies the Sevottam symbol.

head: Core module
Focus
rows: Responsive, empathetic redress, regardless of outcome

notes: Seven steps: define services and identify clients; set standards and norms; develop organisational capability; perform to achieve standards; monitor performance; evaluate impact; continuous improvement.

Significance: structured quality management (example: 2025 DARPG National Workshop in Bhopal); citizen-centric culture; sustainable reform; credible self-assessment. Challenges: seen as procedural compliance; fragmented adoption; weak digital integration. Way forward: capacity building and training; link with CPGRAMS, MyGov and dashboards; third-party audits and feedback loops.

SECS.title: RTI Act 2005 and the 2019 Amendment
SECS.story: RTI is not codified but read into Arts 19(1)(a), 21, 39(b), 39(c). The MKSS movement (Janawad, 'Humara Paisa, Humara Hisab') fed the NAC-drafted 2005 Act: maximum disclosure, minimal exemption, appeals, penalties, proactive disclosure. Section 8 exemptions, public authority disputes and the 2019 amendment are the live questions.

prelims: Sweden first RTI (1766); USA second (1966); Shourie Group 1997; FOI Bill 2002 not notified; Tamil Nadu first state 1997
Penalty Rs 250/day up to Rs 25,000
16 types of information within 120 days; PIOs within 100 days; transfer in 5 days; third party notice 10 days; 30 days to respond
Copyright is the only absolute exemption; Act is retrospective; exempt categories released after 20 years
CIC (2013) on political parties; BCCI public authority (CIC, 2018); judiciary covered (SC, 2019)
mains: RTI 2019 amendment: autonomy of Information Commissions (negative and positive)
Public authority disputes: judiciary, political parties, PPP, BCCI
Rights conferred on citizens
lens.close: Maximum disclosure, minimal exemption: the amendment tests whether independence survives executive control.

notes: Sweden: first RTI in 1766; USA second in 1966. Sweden's ombudsman: 1809; India's central ombudsman: 2013 (per this module).

Constitutional locus: not categorically codified; Preamble ideals support it; SC read it into Art 19(1)(a), Art 21, Art 39(b) and 39(c) ('data is the new oil'). Reference cases: Rajnarain 1975; S.P. Gupta 1982. James Madison quote on popular government and popular information.
Spread of democracy; advocacy (World Bank, IMF, Transparency International, NCPRI 1996 led by Aruna Roy, PUCL, ADR). MKSS at Janawad, Rajasthan: slogan 'Humara Paisa, Humara Hisab'.

Benefits: Monopoly + Discretion - Transparency = Corruption; corrects power asymmetry; realises other rights (e.g. Food Security entitlements); citizen participation; corrects trust deficit (information within 30 days); better record keeping and decisions; shields civil servants from unwarranted pressure (documentary proof).

1997 working group under H.D. Shourie produced the Freedom of Information Bill, 2002 (enacted, not implemented/notified; seen as feeble). States acted first: Tamil Nadu 1997. The 2005 bill was prepared by the National Advisory Council, not bureaucrats.

Criteria for a sound regime: wide access (minimal fees, free for BPL); penalties Rs 250 a day up to Rs 25,000 plus disciplinary action; independent appeal (CIC and SICs); maximum disclosure, minimal exemption.
Preamble philosophy: transparency, check corruption, accountability, empowerment, democracy, balanced with genuine confidentiality and efficiency.

All citizens have the right; broad definition of information (records, memos, e-mail, opinions, advice, press releases, circulars, orders, logbooks, contracts, reports, samples, models, electronic data, private-body information held by a public authority). Right includes inspecting work, notes and certified copies, samples, and electronic formats.

Public authority: bodies under the Constitution, Parliament or state law, or by notification; bodies owned, controlled or substantially financed; NGOs substantially financed (term 'substantially' not defined).

head: Contested body
What the handout says
rows: Substantially financed; many judgments brought them in. Law Commission: BCCI public authority; CIC affirmed in 2018
DoPT circular 2013: make information public. DIAL: CIC (2010) held public authority; Delhi HC stayed
2009 Subhash Agrawal petition on Judges' 1997 resolution; SC said apex court not covered; CIC ruled against; Delhi HC sided with CIC; SC in 2019 held the judiciary by and large covered
CIC 2013: recognised parties are public authorities (IT exemptions, free airtime, subsidised land). Not stayed or nullified by courts; parties still do not comply, citing sub judice

notes: Handout flags problematic SC observations: RBI need not disclose banks' risk-evaluation or inspection reports; RTI has created 'fear psychosis and paralysis'; civil servants' personal status, professional records, assets and liabilities and interviewers' names beyond RTI. Objections to parties' coverage: free associations, no direct tax money, no infrastructure, may be used against each other.

Catalogued, indexed, computerised records; publish 16 types of information within 120 days and update yearly; suo motu disclosure; designate PIOs within 100 days; transfer misdirected requests within 5 days; third-party information after notice and hearing (10 days).

Sovereignty, security, strategic, scientific, economic interests, foreign relations, incitement; court-forbidden or contempt; breach of legislative privilege; commercial confidence, trade secrets, IP (unless larger public interest); fiduciary relationship; foreign government confidences; endangering safety or identifying sources; impeding investigation; Cabinet papers (decisions, reasons and material to be made public after the matter is complete); personal information unrelated to public activity.

Public interest override: access allowed where disclosure outweighs the harm, notwithstanding the Official Secrets Act 1923. Copyright of a person other than the State is the only absolute exemption. Information that cannot be denied to Parliament cannot be denied to citizens.

Second Schedule: intelligence and security agencies are outside the Act, but corruption and human rights violation information must be given (human rights only with the Information Commission's approval). CBI and NIA were added by executive order.

Act overrides the OSA; courts barred from suits other than appeals under the Act; wholly retrospective; exempted information released after 20 years (except Cabinet decisions, legislative privilege, and sovereignty, security, strategic, scientific, economic, foreign relations and incitement categories).

Choose the medium and the language (English, Hindi, local); help in writing; no reason need be given; immediate notice of transfer; assistance for disabled; fees waived for BPL and if time limits are missed; reasons for rejection, appeal period and appellate authority; complaint to CIC/SIC for no PIO/APIO access, refusal, no response in time, unreasonable fee, incomplete, misleading or false information.

head: Key amendment
Effect
rows: Centre decides CIC and ICs' tenure; five-year term removed
Centre fixes; delinked from CEC and ECs
CIC clarified as statutory, not constitutional

notes: Negative: executive overreach; public distrust; federal dilution (SICs). Positive: administrative flexibility; fiscal discipline; policy alignment. Reflection: balances efficiency with independence but risks executive overreach; impact depends on how responsibly the government exercises the powers.

SECS.title: CIC, RTI Issues, Impact and 2nd ARC
SECS.story: CIC composition, selection and removal are spelled out, with the 2019 Rules making tenure 3 years or age 65 and salary Rs 2.5 lakh. The weakness is delivery: pendency, penalty gaps, vacancies, awareness and record keeping. 2nd ARC prescribes structure, funding and secrecy reform.

prelims: CIC + up to 10 ICs; selection: PM, LoP (LS), Union Cabinet Minister nominated by PM
Notified tenure: 3 years or age 65, no reappointment; IC-to-CIC total max 5 years
Salary: CIC Rs 2,50,000, IC Rs 2,25,000 per month
95% penalty gap (Satark Nagrik Sangathan); 2.55 lakh pendency in 26 ICs; avg disposal 1 year 11 months; 21 of 29 ICs filed no report 2019-20
2nd ARC: 1% of flagship funds; 4 regional CIC offices; 50% operating cost for 3 yrs or Rs 1 crore = substantially financed
mains: Issues and challenges in RTI implementation
Impact of RTI
2nd ARC recommendations: OSA repeal, classification, selection of ICs
lens.close: RTI is a means; access is the end, and the gap between them is capacity, will and records.

notes: One Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners; appointed by the President on a committee of the PM (Chair), Leader of Opposition (LS), a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by PM. Eminent persons from law, science, social service, journalism, mass media, public administration. No office of profit, party link or business.
Tenure (RTI Rules 2019): notified by the Centre: 3 years or age 65, whichever is earlier; no reappointment; an IC elevated as CIC cannot exceed 5 years in total.
Salary (Rules 2019): delinked from CEC/EC parity. CIC Rs 2,50,000 per month; IC Rs 2,25,000.

Removal: proved misbehaviour or incapacity after a Supreme Court inquiry (if referred by the President). Without SC inquiry: insolvency, conviction involving moral turpitude, paid employment, unfitness of body or mind, prejudicial financial interest.

Gap between RTI as a means and access as an end; bureaucratic mindset; no specific budget (2nd ARC: 1% of flagship funds); absence of political will; limited awareness (APWC study: 12% of women, 26% of men, 13% rural, 33% urban); vague terms; ICs dominated by retired bureaucrats.

Penal provisions rarely applied: Satark Nagrik Sangathan: penalty not imposed in 95% of cases where due. No organic CIC-SIC relationship. PIO duties added without incentive; juniors appointed as PIOs; poor record keeping; abuse of Schedule II; IC orders not implemented (no contempt powers).

Pendency: an estimated 40-60 lakh RTI requests a year; 2.55 lakh pending in 26 ICs; vacancies; average disposal 1 year 11 months; COVID worsened it. 21 of 29 ICs had not submitted the 2019-20 report; AP and Telangana SICs none since 2017; Odisha since 2015-16. Waning interest of media and activists.

A grievance redressal tool as well; exposed corruption, wasteful expenditure, scams, false narratives, recruitment results and marks; rural access largely through NGOs; became a national movement aiding the Right to Food and Education; more successful for personally relevant information than for controversial public-interest information.
Repeal the Official Secrets Act; replace oath of secrecy with oath of transparency; periodic review of the Second Schedule.
Norms set by the Ministry of Home and not public. Public Records Act 1993: 5-year review of Top Secret, Secret, Confidential items for declassification.
Selection: committee to include the CJI instead of the Union Cabinet Minister; at least half of ICs from non-civil-service background.

Access: 4 regional CIC offices; nodal PIO where more than one PIO; PIOs at least Deputy Secretary or Director level in the central secretariat; flexible payment (stamps, postal orders); district single-window agency; free print suo motu disclosure; independent public records office; 1% of flagship fund for 5 years; training beyond PIOs; awareness through credible NGOs; National Coordination Committee chaired by the CIC; 'substantially financed' = 50% of operating costs for 3 years or at least Rs 1 crore; check frivolous complaints.

SECS.title: The Problem of Corruption
SECS.src: Handout only; three PYQs map here (2014, 2016, 2019)
SECS.story: Corruption is hard to define (TI: private abuse of public office; the Elephant Test), comes in many types, and harms society, economy, politics, security and foreign standing. Its causes are psycho-social, economic, legal, administrative and political, and measuring it is imperfect.

prelims: TI definition; Elephant Test; CPI since 1995 (0 most corrupt, 100 least)
Black, white, grey; grass-eating vs meat-eating; coercive vs collusive; retail vs policy
Legal factors: Art 311, PCA Sec 19, CrPC Sec 197, DSPE Sec 6A (Vineet Narain 1997; struck down 2014), PCA Sec 17A (2018)
2020 CPI: New Zealand, Denmark least corrupt; Somalia, South Sudan last; Bhutan 24th, USA 25th, Botswana 35th, China 78th, Pakistan 124th
Global Corruption Barometer; PETS (World Bank); Paulo Mauro: investment differential up to 12%
mains: Behaviour that harms public interest (non-performance of duty as corruption)
Factors behind corruption: psycho-social, economic, legal, administrative, political
Implications: social, economic, political, security, international
Why poverty is not the only cause; powerful and affluent also corrupt
lens.close: Corruption is an elephant: recognised by society even when it cannot be defined, and fed by opportunity and discretion.

notes: Corruption is as old as civilisation; Kautilya's Arthashastra lists ways a civil servant can be corrupt and the measures to contain it.
Is a gift a bribe? Consider intent of the donor, expectation of the recipient, timing, value, the legal framework, and social acceptability.
Cultural differences: old school ties (UK); regulated lobbying (USA); Blat (Russia, from the Soviet Union); Guanxi (China).

Public only, or private sector too? Too wide a net dilutes focus; if government is incorruptible, private corruption falls. Transparency International: 'private abuse of public office'; the Elephant Test: hard to define, but society knows it when it sees it.

head: Pair
Meaning
rows: Whole society agrees it is corrupt and intolerable
Recognised as corrupt but tolerated (speed money)
Sections of society differ on whether it is corrupt
Does not seek bribes but will not refuse one
Citizen must bribe to get his due; official extorts
Official and bribe-giver collude against public interest
Crony capitalism and state capture; shaping policy for illegal benefit

notes: Behaviour that harms public interest: lethargy; dereliction or negligence of duty; repeated carelessness; non-punctuality; subjective interpretation of public interest; favouritism and nepotism; communalism, casteism, lynching, regional bias.
Social: vertical and horizontal divisions; insecurity (people stop reporting crime); endangers lives (building collapse, fires, false certificates); erodes social fabric.

Economic: reduced aid (African examples); less investment (Paulo Mauro: up to 12% differential); acts as an extra tax; lower revenue; diverted expenditure; poorer efficiency; distorted competition and crony capitalism; brain drain and capital flight; harder entry into international clubs (Eastern Europe and the EU); environmental damage.

Political and legal: raises officials' discretion; money power; pork-barreling; despair favours extremist politicians; mass unrest (India Against Corruption); radical tendencies (Left extremism, North-East insurgency fed by corruption and poor development).

Security: security forces aiding laundering, drugs, trafficking, arms; poor defence procurement quality. International: Magnitsky Act, 2012 (US law, soured ties with Russia); German car insurance (1990s) thefts and smuggling with corrupt officials, premium spike, diplomatic row.
Revisionism: a minority school holding some corruption is not bad because it speeds a lethargic, low-paid bureaucracy.

Psycho-social: need for THYMOS (respect/recognition) and low self-worth; societal shaming of government employees; Squirrel Nuts Syndrome (close to retirement); Opportunity theory (reduce opportunities); religious context (Protestant areas less corrupt); long history; no popular sanction against it; social evils (dowry, lavish weddings).

Economic: poor pay at upper levels (raising pay alone may not dent it); consumerism; licence-permit-quota raj to clearance raj; MNCs' willingness and ability to bribe; business houses outbidding each other.

Legal: Article 311 makes dismissal hard; PCA Sec 19 needs appointing authority's sanction before prosecution; CrPC Sec 197 sanction for non-corruption offences in discharge of duty. Both protect honest officers but are misused.

DSPE Act Sec 6A chain: a single directive required sanction for preliminary inquiry and investigation against Joint Secretary and above; struck down in Vineet Narain (1997); DSPE Act amended to make it law as Sec 6A; Sec 6A struck down in 2014 (equality); PCA amended 2018, Sec 17A: permission needed for preliminary inquiry for all public servants except when caught red-handed.
Also: delayed prosecution; no effective whistleblower law; inadequate autonomy of CBI and CVC.
Administrative: procedural complexity creates middlemen; red tape; weak internal grievance machinery; peer pressure; resistance to reform; politicised transfers and plum postings; culture of secrecy.

Political: absence of political will (repeated Lokpal delay); criminalisation of politics; no neutrality; low voter maturity and the TINA factor; money power in elections and weak disclosure norms for party funding.

Official statistics (weak where prosecution is weak). Perception surveys: TI's Corruption Perception Index, annual since 1995, 0 = most corrupt, 100 = least; 2020 CPI (released 2021): New Zealand and Denmark least corrupt, Somalia and South Sudan last; Bhutan 24th, USA 25th, Botswana 35th, China 78th, Pakistan 124th. Critiques: based on experts and business leaders; perception, not objective; sources change; country count varies so ranks are not comparable.

Experiential: TI's Global Corruption Barometer (not annual, regional); in Asia Japan least corrupt and India most corrupt among 17 countries. Tracking: World Bank's PETS. Content analysis of media (crude).

SECS.title: Tackling Corruption and Social Audit
SECS.src: Handout only; 2021 PYQ direct, 2016 participation PYQ partial
SECS.story: Corruption is a wicked problem: it can be controlled, not eliminated. The toolkit spans stick, carrot, administrative, radical and international measures. Social audit is the participatory tool: public hearings that need a sound RTI regime, with AP's SSAAT as the model.

prelims: Stick/carrot/admin/radical measures with country examples (Botswana, Singapore CPIB, Hong Kong ICAC, South Africa, Georgia, Peru, Romania)
CAG covers only 25% of auditable units yearly; procurement 30% of GDP; 2012 bill lapsed
International: FCPA 1977, UK Bribery Act 2010, OECD 1997, UNCAC 2003, FATF 1989
Social audit: Meghalaya 2017 Act; AP SSAAT; Karnataka rotation after 3 cycles; Chhattisgarh wall writing; Swaraj Abhiyan 2016; MKSS jan sunwai
mains: Stick vs carrot measures; why fragmented agencies fail
Features, significance and issues of social audit; how to strengthen
Success stories: AP, Jharkhand, MKSS, Bengaluru CRCs, benchmarking
lens.close: Make demand-side pressure real: audits only work when information flows freely.

notes: 'Wicked problem': despite PCA, Lokpal, CVC Act, corruption persists; more laws signal systemic inefficiency; it can only be controlled.

Prosecution: higher conviction deters (Botswana); India's delays and lenient punishment weaken deterrence; harsh penalties (China) unsuitable without rule of law. Stings and entrapment: admissibility unclear; natural stings (citizen recordings) should be admissible; Sweden restrictive. Tighten laws: 2018 amendments diluted PCA. Asset declaration with lifestyle monitoring. Effective agencies: India is fragmented (CVC, CBI, Lokpal, ED); Singapore CPIB and Hong Kong ICAC succeed with one agency. Shaming and blacklisting (South Africa); forfeiture of pensions.
Substantial pay increase paired with enforcement; citizen helplines (Delhi anti-corruption hotline) needing whistleblower and witness protection.

Job rotation (Kautilya); stronger auditing (CAG covers 25% of auditable units yearly); procurement norms and a Public Procurement Law (procurement 30% of GDP; 2012 bill lapsed); digitisation; CCTV in high-risk zones.
Disband departments (Georgia's Traffic Police, 2004); gender balance (Peru); monetising bribes (Romania's conscription policy; controversial); general amnesty (50% surrender of black money; debated).

US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (1977), UK Bribery Act (2010); OECD Anti-Bribery Convention (1997); UNCAC (2003); FATF (1989); Interpol IGEC; WTO inaction; global financial transparency against banking havens.

Critique of the global industry: West ignored corruption until the 1990s; anti-corruption became a geopolitical tool; NGO vested interests, data over impact; cultural imperialism concerns. Alternatives: spiritual education; Integrity Recognition Certificates for honest officers (must be insulated from politicisation).

Scheme details (financial and non-financial) shared with beneficiaries on a public platform (Jan Sunwai, public hearing, Gram Sabha), so people can hold bureaucracy and Panchayat leaders accountable. Key: a sound access-to-information regime.
Features: multi-perspective; regular; comparative (time and space); strengthens the demand side and indirectly targets supply-side weakness.

Significance: participation; benefits reach the target; social capital; identifies civil servants' HR and training needs; highlights development concerns; transparency and anti-corruption; better future programmes.

Issues: not in mainstream policy discourse; statutory in very few programmes (NREGA is one); lack of trained auditors; opposition from vested interests. Symptom-cause point: audit across cause-effect layers, not surface symptoms alone (e.g. plague awareness drive without fixing sanitation).
Legal and institutional: national law inspired by Meghalaya's 2017 Act; independent units like Andhra Pradesh's SSAAT; support CAG and PRIs.
Stakeholders: Gram Sabha awareness; auditor training; NGO and media; recognition for participants. Digital: portals; proactive disclosure; unified guidelines.
Best practices: Chhattisgarh links audits to grievance redress and uses wall writing; Karnataka rotates audit teams after every three audit cycles.

head: Success story
Detail
rows: Autonomous society; village resource persons; crores of wage misappropriation recovered; World Bank called it a global best practice
MGNREGA, PDS, pensions; ghost beneficiaries, delays, ration diversion exposed; SC in Swaraj Abhiyan (2016) appreciated social audits
1990s jan sunwais revealed leakages; led to the RTI Act 2005
Civil society report cards on water, hospitals, transport; bribery fell, satisfaction rose; 2003 study
Compare service costs (e.g. cost per km of road); disclosure pressures inefficient bodies

SECS.title: CBI and CVC
SECS.src: Handout only; the 2021 CBI-consent PYQ is only partly covered (no state-consent material in the notes)
SECS.story: The CBI (SPE 1941, DSPE Act 1946, named 1963) is politicised ('caged parrot') despite Vineet Narain (1997). The CVC (Santhanam, 1964; statutory 2003) superintends CBI on PCA cases but depends on it and cannot prosecute.

prelims: CBI: SPE 1941; DSPE Act 1946; name 1963; four divisions; conviction rate 67% vs 30-40%; no suo motu jurisdiction
Vineet Narain 1997: CVC supervises CBI; Director's min. tenure 2 years; committee (PM, LoP, CJI); single directive struck down; DoPT policy only
CVC: 1964 executive; statutory 2003; CVC + max 2 VCs; term 4 years or 65; pay = UPSC Chair/members
PJ Thomas 2011: consensus not majority in selection committee
CVC Chair heads committee for ED Director and CBI officers SP and above
mains: Issues in CBI functioning and Vineet Narain directions
CVC powers, issues and suggestions
Institutional framework against corruption
lens.close: Autonomy of anti-graft agencies is the weak link: independence of selection, tenure, prosecution and staff.

notes: Sec 203 BNS (Sec 169 IPC): civil servant illegally acquiring property; Sec 316 BNS (Sec 409 IPC): criminal breach of trust by a public servant (as printed). DSPE Act 1946 (CBI); RPA 1951 Sec 123; PCA 1988; Benami Properties Act 1988; PMLA 2003; CVC Act; RTI 2005; Lokayukta Acts; Lokpal Act 2013; Whistleblower Act 2014; time-bound service delivery laws.
Institutions: CBI, CVC, state ACBs and vigilance wings, CAG, Lokayuktas, Lokpal, ED (PMLA and FEMA), banking ombudsman, consumer courts, three-tier judiciary.
Special Police Establishment 1941; statutory backing by DSPE Act 1946; named CBI in 1963. Divisions: Anti-Corruption; Special Crimes; Economic Offences; Banking and Security Frauds.

Issues: politicisation ('caged parrot', a former SC judge); about one-third posts vacant; conviction rate 67% vs 30-40% for other agencies, but low in high-profile cases; sanction delays (Sec 19 PCA, Sec 197 CrPC); no suo motu jurisdiction (cases transferred to it).

CVC to superintend CBI on PCA cases; minimum guaranteed tenure for the Director (2 years under DSPE Act; later extendable up to 5 in yearly steps by ordinance); Director chosen by a committee: PM, Leader of Opposition (or largest opposition party leader), CJI; Single Directive struck down; DoPT sets only overall policy, not day-to-day investigations; Director's transfer by the same committee.

Set up in 1964 as an executive body on the K. Santhanam Committee (1962); statutory in 2003 under the CVC Act. Apex vigilance institution free of executive control; advises on planning, reviewing, reforming vigilance. Central Vigilance Commissioner + not more than two Vigilance Commissioners.

Selection: from All India or Central Services, and from CPSU officers (not more than two from the two categories, so at least one from each). Committee: PM, Home Minister, Leader of Opposition (government has the final say). P.J. Thomas case (2011): government majority made the LoP's role pointless; selection must follow consensus of all members, not majority (only for this appointment).

Term: 4 years for CVC and VCs; retirement age 65; no reappointment; a VC can become CVC but total stay not above 4 years; barred from UT administrator, diplomatic and other presidential-warrant posts; no office of profit. Pay: CVC equals UPSC Chairperson, VCs equal UPSC members; charged to the Consolidated Fund; cannot be altered to disadvantage. Removal: proved misbehaviour or incapacity on SC reference; plus insolvency, moral turpitude, private employment, infirmity, prejudicial financial interest.

Functions and powers: superintend CBI on corruption cases (Vineet Narain) and give directions; inquire on Central Government reference or on complaints against Group A, All India Service officers and equivalent CPSU officials; review DSPE investigations and pending sanction applications; tender advice; superintend vigilance in ministries; powers of a civil court; mandatory consultation on vigilance and disciplinary rules; CVC chairs the committee recommending the ED Director (and Deputy Director and above); chairs the committee recommending CBI officers of SP level and above (not Director). Annual report to the President, laid before Parliament.
Issues: dependence on a politicised CBI; no independent prosecution powers and sanction delays; non-cooperative government; poor engagement with civil society.

Suggestions: independent investigative and prosecution powers (2nd ARC: functional autonomy); 3-6 month statutory timeline for sanction (TI India: over 70% of sanctions pending beyond 6 months in 2023); binding oversight over vigilance administration; manpower (less than 50% of sanctioned staff, over 1,500 organisations per CVC 2023 report); civil society participation (South Korea ACRC); binding recommendations; wider selection panel (judiciary or experts).

SECS.title: Lokpal in India
SECS.story: The Ombudsman began in Sweden (1809). India's First ARC proposed a two-tier model; the bill was first introduced in 1968, passed in 2013, and the Lokpal constituted in 2019. States' Lokayuktas show the weaknesses: no standard design, 'paper tigers', abolition by governments.

prelims: 9-member body; 50% judicial; 50% affirmative action; age 45+; 5 years or 70; salary CJI/SC judge
Selection committee: PM, Speaker, LoP, CJI/nominee, eminent jurist; search committee of 7
PM covered partially (not public order, security, atomic energy, space; full bench two-thirds)
Removal reference signed by 100 MPs; 60 days preliminary inquiry; 7-year limitation
Maharashtra first Lokayukta (1971); Odisha 1992, Haryana 1999 abolished
mains: Should the PM be covered? 2nd ARC arguments and counter-arguments
Issues with Lokpal; functioning since 2019
Lokpal is not a panacea
lens.close: No single body can cure a hydra: Lokpal works only inside a multi-pronged strategy.

notes: Ombudsman: Sweden 1809; UK Parliamentary Commissioner 1967; USA in some states (Hawaii, Oregon, Nebraska), not federal. First ARC: two-tier: Lokpal for Secretary-rank and above at Union and State levels; Union Lokayukta for lower officials; State Lokayuktas in states.
India: first bill 1968; Act 2013; Lokpal constituted 2019 with Justice P.C. Ghose as Chairperson of the nine-member body. Maharashtra first state Lokayukta (1971).

Flooded with complaints; poor effectiveness; inter-state differences (qualifications, tenure, powers, suo motu, no separate agency); survival depends on state government (Odisha abolished it by ordinance in 1992; Haryana in 1999); recommendatory 'paper tigers'; corruption within; misused against political opponents.

Composition: nine members including the Chairperson. Chairperson: a present or former CJI or SC judge, or an eminent person with 25 years' experience in vigilance, anti-corruption, law, finance, administration, management. Eight members: half judicial (SC judge or High Court Chief Justice), half non-judicial (eminent, 25 years). 50% affirmative action: SC, ST, OBC, minorities, women.
Conditions: not an MP, MLA, MLC; no local body membership; minimum age 45; not removed or dismissed from government service; no office of profit, business or profession; no party affiliation.

Appointment by the President on a committee: PM (Chair), Lok Sabha Speaker, Leader of Opposition (LS) (silent on a missing LoP), CJI or nominated SC judge, eminent jurist chosen by the four. A search committee of 7 shortlists, with 50% reservation; the selection committee may go beyond its names.

Tenure: 5 years or age 70; no reappointment, except a member elevated to Chairperson within the 5-year limit. Salary: Chairperson equals CJI; members equal SC judge. Disabilities: like the CVC plus ineligible for any election for 5 years.
Structure: Inquiry Wing (Director of Inquiry), Prosecution Wing (Director of Prosecution), Secretary.

notes.h: Should the Prime Minister be covered?

notes: 2nd ARC opposed: would cripple administration during investigation; foreign powers might exploit it; PM already covered by the PCA 1988. Counter: CBI works under DoPT, hence the PM, which would hamper probes; PM should lead by example (some Lokayuktas cover Chief Ministers); Article 361 exempts only President and Governors.

Act covers PM partially: no inquiry into PM decisions on public order, internal and external security, atomic energy, space; the full bench by two-thirds majority must approve initiating an inquiry or investigation.

PM, Union Ministers, MPs, Group A-D officials, and bodies funded by government above Rs 10 lakh a year. Any individual may complain for PCA offences. Preliminary inquiry via the Inquiry Wing, CVC or agencies like CBI; explanation sought from the public servant; complaints against Groups C and D referred to the CVC; preliminary inquiry within 60 days.

After the report and hearing: full investigation, departmental proceedings, close the case, or proceed against a false complainant. A bench of at least 3 members decides on sanction. Lokpal replaces the appointing authority in sanctions under CrPC Sec 197 and PCA Sec 19. Powers of search, seizure, attachment, and civil court powers; superintendence over CBI for cases it refers.

Removal: on misbehaviour by SC reference signed by at least 100 MPs; President on other grounds (insolvency, private employment, infirmity, prejudicial financial interest). Annual asset declarations; annual report with a memorandum explaining rejected recommendations; 7-year limitation for complaints.
Too wide jurisdiction; convoluted appointment; PM only partly covered; 7-year limit; scope may intimidate NGOs; delays in appointment.

Functioning since 2019: allegations of emasculation by legislation; delayed complaint-form rules, asset disclosure rules, preliminary inquiry and investigation rules; wings not set up by 2020; by Sept 2019 disposed of 1,000 of 1,065 complaints; complaints fell from 1,427 (2019-20) to 110 (2020-21) to 12 till August 2021-22.

2nd ARC: give Lokpal and Lokayuktas constitutional status; Rashtriya Lok Ayukta for Union Ministers, MPs and State Chief Ministers; State Lokayukta for state ministers and legislators; CVC for civil servants; a Local Bodies Ombudsman.

Not a panacea: hydra-headed corruption needs multi-pronged strategy; huge bureaucracy; petty complaints need departmental handling; inadequate judicial process; lacking citizen empowerment and willingness to complain.

SECS.title: Whistleblower Protection and the PCA 1988
SECS.story: The 2014 Act has no anonymity, narrow safeguards and a lapsed 2015 amendment bill that would have let the Official Secrets Act override it. The PCA 1988 covers all public servants; the 2018 amendment criminalised bribe-giving, raised penalties and added Sec 17A.

prelims: Competent authority: PM (Union Ministers), CM (state ministers), Presiding Officer (legislators), CVC (civil servants)
No anonymous complaints; frivolous complaint penalised with 2-year jail
2015 amendment bill lapsed: OSA to override the Act
SEBI tipping mechanism: reward up to Rs 1 crore
PCA 2018: bribe-giving an offence; 7-day complaint defence; jail 3 to 7 years; trial in 2 years, max 4; Sec 17A extends to retired servants
mains: Challenges with the Whistleblower Act and measures to strengthen it
2nd ARC and Law Commission framework
Why the 2018 PCA amendment is both strengthening and diluting
lens.close: A whistleblower law without anonymity protects the disclosure but not the discloser.

notes: Anyone can be a whistleblower regarding any public body. Disclosure to the competent authority: PM for Union Ministers, Chief Minister for state ministers, Presiding Officer for legislators, CVC for civil servants. No anonymous complaints. CVC can issue directions for protection. Frivolous complaints: 2-year jail.
2015 amendment bill (lapsed): proposed that the Official Secrets Act 1923 would override the Act.

No anonymity (murder of Satyendra Dubey, who reported corruption in the NHAI); weak organisational implementation and awareness; inadequate protection against victimisation; yet complaints rise (2018: over 3,500 complaints to NSE-listed companies).

2nd ARC: stronger law covering public and private sectors. Law Commission framework: confidentiality and anonymity; protection against victimisation and bodily harm; coverage of corporate whistleblowers. SEBI's tipping mechanism: rewards up to Rs 1 crore for actionable information on insider trading, with confidentiality.

Covers all public servants: anyone in government pay or service; PSU employees; local body functionaries; judges; office-bearers of government-funded cooperatives; PSC members; employees of central and state universities; deemed university employees (SC, 2020); anyone performing a public duty by virtue of office, including MPs and MLAs.

Giving a bribe is explicitly an offence; in coercive corruption, a complaint within 7 days frees the giver from guilt. Sec 17A extended to retired civil servants. Original Sec 13(1)(d) (decision benefiting a commercial organisation against public interest) diluted. Jail from 3 to 7 years. Trial in 2 years, up to 4. Provisions for prosecuting commercial organisations and for attachment or confiscation of property.

MCQ.q: Which was the first province to set up a Provincial Public Service Commission?
MCQ.e: Madras, in 1929 (M1 p.3). The 1919 Act made provincial commissions optional, not mandatory.

MCQ.q: The Federal Public Service Commission was set up in:
MCQ.e: The 1919 Act only provided for it; it was set up in 1926 on the Lee Commission (1924) recommendation. The 1935 Act created FPSC, PPSC and JPSC types.

MCQ.q: Which article provides for the creation of All India Services?
MCQ.e: Article 312. Art 309 covers recruitment and conditions, 315 the PSCs, 323A administrative tribunals.

MCQ.q: The number of All India Services moved from:
MCQ.e: Nine in 1909, four in 1924, two in 1947 (M1 p.7). Today India has three: IAS, IPS, IFoS.

MCQ.q: In the T.S.R. Subramanian case (2013) the Supreme Court recommended:
o: Minimum tenure in key posts, Civil Services Boards, avoiding verbal orders
Direct recruitment to all Group A posts
MCQ.e: Minimum guaranteed tenure, Civil Services Boards on postings and transfers, no action on verbal orders, and a comprehensive Civil Services Law (M1 p.9). Repealing Art 311 was a 2nd ARC suggestion.

MCQ.q: Under the RTI Act 2005, the only absolute exemption is:
o: Infringement of copyright subsisting in a person other than the State
MCQ.e: Copyright of a non-State person. Other exemptions in Sec 8 can be overridden where public interest outweighs harm (M1 p.34).

MCQ.q: Which pairing from the RTI Act is correct?
o: Transfer of a misdirected request: within 5 days
Notice to a third party: 30 days
Publish 16 types of information: within 100 days
MCQ.e: Transfer within 5 days. Third-party notice is 10 days; PIOs are designated within 100 days; 16 types of information published within 120 days (M1 p.34).

MCQ.q: As notified under the RTI Rules 2019, the tenure of the CIC and Information Commissioners is:
MCQ.e: 3 years or age 65, whichever is earlier, with no reappointment; IC-to-CIC total cannot exceed 5 years (M1 p.36).

MCQ.q: Which of these was NOT part of the Vineet Narain (1997) directions?
o: CVC to superintend the CBI on PCA cases
Minimum tenure for the CBI Director
Director chosen by a committee including the CJI
CBI to have suo motu jurisdiction
MCQ.e: The handout says the CBI has no suo motu jurisdiction and handles transferred cases (M2 p.12). The other three were directed.

MCQ.q: The Central Vigilance Commission was set up in 1964 on the recommendation of the:
MCQ.e: K. Santhanam Committee on Prevention of Corruption (set up 1962). It became statutory under the CVC Act 2003 (M2 p.13).

MCQ.q: A reference to the Supreme Court for removal of a Lokpal member on misbehaviour must be signed by at least:
MCQ.e: At least 100 Members of Parliament (M2 p.18).

MCQ.q: Under the Lokpal Act 2013, the Prime Minister is:
o: Partly covered: no inquiry into decisions on public order, security, atomic energy, space; full bench two-thirds majority to begin
MCQ.e: Partial coverage with those exclusions and a two-thirds full-bench majority (M2 p.17).

MCQ.q: Under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014:
o: Anonymous complaints are not entertained, and frivolous complaints attract 2-year jail
The Official Secrets Act is overridden
Only civil servants can be whistleblowers
MCQ.e: No anonymous complaints; frivolous ones face 2 years (M2 p.19). The OSA-override was the lapsed 2015 amendment bill; anyone can be a whistleblower.

MCQ.q: Which is true of the Prevention of Corruption Amendment Act, 2018?
o: Giving a bribe is not an offence
Jail term cut from 7 to 3 years
Sec 17A requires permission for preliminary inquiry, except when caught red-handed
Retired civil servants are excluded from Sec 17A
MCQ.e: Sec 17A applies to all public servants except those caught red-handed and extends to retired servants; jail rose from 3 to 7 years; bribe-giving is an offence (M2 p.6, 20).

MCQ.q: In Transparency International's Corruption Perception Index (since 1995), a score of:
o: Ranks are comparable across all years
MCQ.e: 0 = most corrupt, 100 = least. It is perception-based, and country count changes so ranks are not comparable (M2 p.7).

MAINSQ.q: Evaluate Mission Karmayogi as a shift from rules-based to roles-based civil services management.

sk.i: Launched in 2020 as the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building.
b: Components: iGOT Karmayogi, competency frameworks, outcome-based performance management, SPV Karmayogi Bharat, Capacity Building Commission
Gains: competency over tenure, real-time feedback beyond ACRs, on-demand training
Challenges: lateral-entrant integration, mindset shift, Centre-State coordination, digital access
Link to Aarambh: Commitment, Character, Conduct
sk.c: Success depends on continuous implementation, not a one-time launch.

MAINSQ.q: Should the Prime Minister be brought under the Lokpal? Examine in light of the Lokpal Act 2013.

sk.i: The Act covers the PM partially.
b: 2nd ARC against: cripples administration, foreign exploitation, PCA already applies
For: CBI works under DoPT; lead by example; Art 361 exempts only President and Governors
Act: no inquiry on public order, security, atomic energy, space; full-bench two-thirds majority
sk.c: Partial coverage balances accountability against continuity, but leaves the main objection unanswered.

MAINSQ.q: Should civil servants have the right to strike? Discuss with reference to the Essential Defence Services Bill 2021.

sk.i: The Bill barred strikes in essential defence services including 41 ordnance factories.
b: For: collective protest, protection from exploitation, last resort
Against: public interest (loaded gun), model citizens, government as fair employer
First ARC (1966): penal offence; SC: no fundamental, statutory or equitable right
sk.c: Distinguish essential from non-essential services rather than ban or permit across the board.

MAINSQ.q: Sevottam is more than a certification. Discuss its significance and the challenges in implementation.

sk.i: 2nd ARC concept, launched 2006; BIS standard IS 15700:2005.
b: Three modules and seven steps
Significance: structured quality management, citizen-centric culture, continuous improvement, self-assessment
Challenges: seen as compliance, fragmented adoption, weak digital integration
Way forward: training, link to CPGRAMS and MyGov, third-party audits
sk.c: Sevottam works when it is a management system, not a badge.

MAINSQ.q: How can the success of Andhra Pradesh's social audit model be scaled up nationally?

sk.i: AP's SSAAT is an autonomous society that trained village resource persons.
b: Result: crores of wage misappropriation recovered; World Bank global best practice
Scale: national law on Meghalaya 2017 lines; independent audit units; PRI capacity
Add: trained auditors, rotation of audit teams (Karnataka), wall writing and grievance link (Chhattisgarh), digital portals
sk.c: Independence of auditors and access to information decide whether audits scale.
